/-!
# Henson graph

For $i \geq 3$, the Henson graph $G_i$ is the unique countable homogeneous graph that contains
no $i$-vertex clique but contains every finite $K_i$-free graph as an induced subgraph. Here a
graph is *homogeneous* if every isomorphism between finite induced subgraphs extends to an
automorphism of the whole graph. The first of these graphs, $G_3$, is also called the homogeneous
triangle-free graph or the universal triangle-free graph.

Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems asks: *do the Henson graphs have the finite model
property?* That is, does every first-order sentence in the language of graphs that holds in $G_i$
also hold in some finite graph? In other words, is $G_i$ pseudofinite? The case $i = 3$ is a
well-known question of Cherlin about the generic triangle-free graph.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Henson graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henson_graph)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [He71] C. Ward Henson, *A family of countable homogeneous graphs*,
  Pacific Journal of Mathematics 38 (1971), 69–83.
- [Ch11] G. Cherlin, *Two problems on homogeneous structures, revisited*, in: Model Theoretic
  Methods in Finite Combinatorics, Contemporary Mathematics 558, AMS (2011), 319–415.
-/

structure IsHensonGraph (i : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop where
  countable : Countable V
  cliqueFree : G.CliqueFree i
  universal : ∀ (W : Type) [Finite W] (H : SimpleGraph W), H.CliqueFree i → Nonempty (H ↪g G)
  isUltrahomogeneous : letI := G.structure; Language.graph.IsUltrahomogeneous V
blocks.docstring:
A simple graph `G` on the vertex type `V` is a *Henson graph* $G_i$ if `V` is countable, `G`
contains no clique on `i` vertices, `G` contains every finite $K_i$-free graph as an induced
subgraph, and `G` is homogeneous, i.e. every isomorphism between finite induced subgraphs of `G`
extends to an automorphism of `G`.

Homogeneity is expressed via `FirstOrder.Language.IsUltrahomogeneous` for the structure
`G.structure` in the language of graphs: since this language is relational, its finitely generated
substructures are exactly the finite induced subgraphs, and its embeddings are exactly the
induced-subgraph embeddings.

For every `i ≥ 3` such a graph exists and is unique up to isomorphism; see [He71].

justification.closest_existing_considered: `FirstOrder.Language.IsFraisseLimit K V` with K the class of finite K_i-free graphs as `Bundled Language.graph.Structure`; rejected as much clunkier to state (age equality of bundled structures), but the homogeneity field does reuse Mathlib's `FirstOrder.Language.IsUltrahomogeneous`.
justification.name: HensonGraph.IsHensonGraph
justification.why_needed: Neither Mathlib nor FormalConjecturesForMathlib defines the Henson graphs (or the Rado graph / Fraïssé limits of concrete classes). Existence of Fraïssé limits is a TODO in Mathlib, so the graph is characterised by its defining properties from the article (countable, K_i-free, universal for finite K_i-free graphs, homogeneous) rather than constructed; by Fraïssé's theorem this pins it down uniquely up to isomorphism.

blocks.docstring:
A simple graph `G` has the *finite model property* (equivalently, `G` is *pseudofinite*) if
every first-order sentence in the language of graphs that holds in `G` also holds in some finite
simple graph. This says exactly that the complete first-order theory of `G` has the finite model
property.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `FirstOrder.Language.completeTheory` together with `Theory.IsSatisfiable`/`Theory.ModelType` (no finiteness variant exists); `FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsFinitelySatisfiable`-style notions are about finite subsets of the theory, not finite models.
justification.name: HensonGraph.HasFiniteModelProperty
justification.why_needed: Mathlib has no notion of the finite model property of a theory or of pseudofinite structures. Defined for a simple graph G as: every `Language.graph.Sentence` realized in `G.structure` is realized in some finite simple graph. For the complete theory Th(G) this is exactly the finite model property (every finite subset of Th(G) has a finite model) and exactly pseudofiniteness of G.

blocks.name: HasFiniteModelProperty
blocks.text:
/-- A simple graph `G` has the *finite model property* (equivalently, `G` is *pseudofinite*) if
every first-order sentence in the language of graphs that holds in `G` also holds in some finite
simple graph. This says exactly that the complete first-order theory of `G` has the finite model
property. -/
def HasFiniteModelProperty (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ φ : Language.graph.Sentence, (letI := G.structure; V ⊨ φ) →
    ∃ (W : Type) (H : SimpleGraph W), Finite W ∧ (letI := H.structure; W ⊨ φ)

blocks.code:
@[category test, AMS 3 5]
theorem hasFiniteModelProperty_of_finite [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    HasFiniteModelProperty G :=
  fun _ hφ => ⟨V, G, inferInstance, hφ⟩
blocks.docstring: Every finite simple graph has the finite model property.

blocks.code:
@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem IsHensonGraph.infinite {i : ℕ} {G : SimpleGraph V} (hi : 2 ≤ i)
    (hG : IsHensonGraph i G) : Infinite V := by
  refine Infinite.of_not_fintype fun _ => ?_
  obtain ⟨f⟩ := hG.universal (Fin (Fintype.card V + 1)) ⊥ (cliqueFree_bot hi)
  have := Fintype.card_le_of_injective f f.injective
  simp at this
blocks.docstring:
A Henson graph $G_i$ with $i \geq 2$ is infinite, since it contains every finite edgeless
graph as an induced subgraph.

claims.decomposer_note: Yes/no question, implicitly quantified over every i ≥ 3: for each Henson graph G_i (the unique countable homogeneous graph that is K_i-free and universal for finite K_i-free graphs), the complete first-order theory of G_i in the language of graphs has the finite model property, i.e. every first-order sentence true in G_i has a finite (graph) model (G_i is pseudofinite); the article never mentions the FMP, so the definition must be supplied from model theory (Cherlin's problem), and the Prop should be stated as ∀ i ≥ 3 with a single answer(sorry) since the plural 'the Henson graphs' asks about all of them.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates agree on the reading (∀ i ≥ 3, every graph satisfying the Wikipedia characterization of G_i — countable, K_i-free, universal for finite K_i-free graphs via induced embeddings `↪g`, homogeneous — is pseudofinite: every `Language.graph` sentence true in it has a finite graph model), with a single answer(sorry) and all quantifiers after it. c01 was chosen as the base because it uses Mathlib's `IsUltrahomogeneous` on `G.structure` (exactly graph homogeneity since `Language.graph` is relational: FG substructures = finite vertex sets, embeddings reflect adjacency), uses Mathlib's `Language.graph`/`SimpleGraph.structure` rather than a bespoke language (unlike c04), keeps definitions in the problem namespace (rather than `_root_` generic defs in a problem file as c02/c05), quantifies over `Type` (avoiding c02/c07's universe-polymorphic theorem), and includes test/API lemmas. Edits: argument order `IsHensonGraph i G`, explicit `W` binder in the universality field, added Cherlin reference (from c07) and expanded docstrings.

context:
In graph theory, the Henson graph Gi is an undirected infinite graph, the unique countable homogeneous graph that does not contain an i-vertex clique but that does contain all Ki-free finite graphs as induced subgraphs. For instance, G3 is a triangle-free graph that contains all finite triangle-free graphs.
These graphs are named after C. Ward Henson, who published a construction for them (for all i ≥ 3) in 1971. The first of these graphs, G3, is also called the homogeneous triangle-free graph or the universal triangle-free graph.

decomposition_objections.text: None. The table's reading (FMP of the complete theory of each G_i, i ≥ 3, single answer; i = 3 as a subordinate special case) matches the standard interpretation of the list entry and Cherlin's problem.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Henson graph

For $i \geq 3$, the Henson graph $G_i$ is the unique countable homogeneous graph that contains
no $i$-vertex clique but contains every finite $K_i$-free graph as an induced subgraph. Here a
graph is *homogeneous* if every isomorphism between finite induced subgraphs extends to an
automorphism of the whole graph. The first of these graphs, $G_3$, is also called the homogeneous
triangle-free graph or the universal triangle-free graph.

Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems asks: *do the Henson graphs have the finite model
property?* That is, does every first-order sentence in the language of graphs that holds in $G_i$
also hold in some finite graph? In other words, is $G_i$ pseudofinite? The case $i = 3$ is a
well-known question of Cherlin about the generic triangle-free graph.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Henson graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henson_graph)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [He71] C. Ward Henson, *A family of countable homogeneous graphs*,
  Pacific Journal of Mathematics 38 (1971), 69–83.
- [Ch11] G. Cherlin, *Two problems on homogeneous structures, revisited*, in: Model Theoretic
  Methods in Finite Combinatorics, Contemporary Mathematics 558, AMS (2011), 319–415.
-/

namespace HensonGraph

open FirstOrder Language SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type}

/-- A simple graph `G` on the vertex type `V` is a *Henson graph* $G_i$ if `V` is countable, `G`
contains no clique on `i` vertices, `G` contains every finite $K_i$-free graph as an induced
subgraph, and `G` is homogeneous, i.e. every isomorphism between finite induced subgraphs of `G`
extends to an automorphism of `G`.

Homogeneity is expressed via `FirstOrder.Language.IsUltrahomogeneous` for the structure
`G.structure` in the language of graphs: since this language is relational, its finitely generated
substructures are exactly the finite induced subgraphs, and its embeddings are exactly the
induced-subgraph embeddings.

For every `i ≥ 3` such a graph exists and is unique up to isomorphism; see [He71]. -/
structure IsHensonGraph (i : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop where
  countable : Countable V
  cliqueFree : G.CliqueFree i
  universal : ∀ (W : Type) [Finite W] (H : SimpleGraph W), H.CliqueFree i → Nonempty (H ↪g G)
  isUltrahomogeneous : letI := G.structure; Language.graph.IsUltrahomogeneous V

/-- A simple graph `G` has the *finite model property* (equivalently, `G` is *pseudofinite*) if
every first-order sentence in the language of graphs that holds in `G` also holds in some finite
simple graph. This says exactly that the complete first-order theory of `G` has the finite model
property. -/
def HasFiniteModelProperty (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ φ : Language.graph.Sentence, (letI := G.structure; V ⊨ φ) →
    ∃ (W : Type) (H : SimpleGraph W), Finite W ∧ (letI := H.structure; W ⊨ φ)

/-- Every finite simple graph has the finite model property. -/
@[category test, AMS 3 5]
theorem hasFiniteModelProperty_of_finite [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    HasFiniteModelProperty G :=
  fun _ hφ => ⟨V, G, inferInstance, hφ⟩

/-- A Henson graph $G_i$ with $i \geq 2$ is infinite, since it contains every finite edgeless
graph as an induced subgraph. -/
@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem IsHensonGraph.infinite {i : ℕ} {G : SimpleGraph V} (hi : 2 ≤ i)
    (hG : IsHensonGraph i G) : Infinite V := by
  refine Infinite.of_not_fintype fun _ => ?_
  obtain ⟨f⟩ := hG.universal (Fin (Fintype.card V + 1)) ⊥ (cliqueFree_bot hi)
  have := Fintype.card_le_of_injective f f.injective
  simp at this

/-- Do the Henson graphs have the finite model property? That is, for every $i \geq 3$, does every
first-order sentence in the language of graphs that holds in the Henson graph $G_i$ also hold in
some finite graph? Since $G_i$ is unique up to isomorphism, the question is stated for every
graph satisfying the defining properties of $G_i$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 3 5]
theorem henson_graph :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ i ≥ 3, ∀ (V : Type) (G : SimpleGraph V), IsHensonGraph i G →
      HasFiniteModelProperty G := by
  sorry

/-- The case $i = 3$ of `henson_graph`, due to Cherlin [Ch11]: does the homogeneous (universal)
triangle-free graph $G_3$ have the finite model property? That is, does every first-order sentence
in the language of graphs that holds in $G_3$ also hold in some finite graph? -/
@[category research open, AMS 3 5]
theorem henson_graph.variants.triangle_free :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (V : Type) (G : SimpleGraph V), IsHensonGraph 3 G →
      HasFiniteModelProperty G := by
  sorry

end HensonGraph

items: The list-page entry is terse; the precise formulation is taken from the article's definition of G_i (unique countable homogeneous K_i-free graph containing all finite K_i-free graphs as induced subgraphs) plus the standard model-theoretic meaning of 'finite model property' for the complete theory Th(G_i): every sentence true in G_i has a finite model (G_i is pseudofinite). This is the sense of Cherlin's question; the alternative reading 'Th(G_i) is axiomatised by its finite models' would be trivially false since Th(G_i) has no finite models, so it is not the intended one.

The finite model is required to be a finite simple graph (rather than an arbitrary finite structure in the graph language). This is equivalent: if φ holds in G one may conjoin the (finitely many) graph axioms, which also hold in G, so any finite model of the conjunction is a graph.

Instead of constructing G_i, the theorem quantifies over all graphs on a `Type` (universe 0) vertex set satisfying `IsHensonGraph G i`. Since such graphs exist (Henson 1971) and are unique up to isomorphism (Fraïssé), and pseudofiniteness is isomorphism-invariant, this is equivalent to the statement about 'the' Henson graph G_i; the quantifier is not vacuous.

Homogeneity is expressed with Mathlib's `FirstOrder.Language.IsUltrahomogeneous Language.graph V` under `G.structure`. In the relational graph language, finitely generated substructures are finite vertex sets and `↪[L]` embeddings preserve and reflect adjacency, so this is exactly 'every isomorphism between finite induced subgraphs extends to an automorphism'.
'Countable' in `IsHensonGraph` allows finite V, following the article's wording; universality forces V to be infinite (proved as the API lemma `IsHensonGraph.infinite`).

Primary statement quantifies over all i ≥ 3 with a single `answer(sorry)`, as the plural 'the Henson graphs' asks about all of them; `answer(True)` means every G_i is pseudofinite, `answer(False)` means some G_i is not.
Two short auxiliary results were added as sanity checks on the bespoke definitions (finite graphs have the FMP; Henson graphs with i ≥ 2 are infinite), tagged `test`/`API`.

reviewer_notes: Interpretation: 'finite model property' is read (per the decomposition notes and Cherlin's problem) as pseudofiniteness of the complete theory of G_i — every first-order sentence in the language of graphs true in G_i has a finite model. The alternative reading 'Th(G_i) is axiomatised by its finite models' is trivially false (Th(G_i) has no finite models), so it cannot be the intended one. Finite models are required to be finite simple graphs (possibly empty W); this is equivalent to allowing arbitrary finite structures or requiring nonemptiness, because the graph axioms and ∃x (x = x) are sentences true in the infinite G_i and can be conjoined to any sentence. c05's 'every finite subset of completeTheory has a finite model' is also equivalent; the sentence-based form was preferred as more direct. G_i is not constructed (no Fraïssé limits/Henson construction in Mathlib); the theorems quantify over all graphs satisfying the characterization, which is non-vacuous (Henson 1971) and legitimate since G_i is unique up to isomorphism and pseudofiniteness is isomorphism-invariant. `Countable V` (not countably infinite) follows the article; infiniteness is forced by universality (API lemma `IsHensonGraph.infinite`). Vertex types are restricted to universe `Type`, harmless for countable graphs. No candidate omitted any slot; no objections to the decomposition were raised, and I concur with it. Final file compiles with only 'declaration uses sorry' warnings.
